utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning Your Honours, good morning everyone in and around the courtroom, this is IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Today is Thursday, the 29th of May, 2008. Good morning to the accused, to the Defence counsel, to Mr. Stringer and to his assistants. Good morning to everyone assisting us in this case and especially to the interpreters. First, I would like to turn to Mr. Coric's counsel. Why is Mr. Coric not in the courtroom today and I would like to ask the same thing of Mr. Ibrisimovic. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I haven't received any specific information as to why Mr. Coric is absent from court today; however, he told me yesterday that he was a bit under the weather, we know what the weather conditions are like, that he had problems with his blood pressure; and I believe he even hinted he might not appear one of these days due to these reasons, so I don't think there is really a reason for concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I don't have any information at this stage about Mr. Pusic but I believe we will be receiving some from the UNDU, I don't think there is reason for concern either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine, Mr. Stringer, you wanted to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you and good morning to Your Honours and counsel and everyone else. Just to be clear for the record, I take it that counsel for Mr. Coric and Pusic have no objection to proceeding today in their absence and I assume that the necessary paperwork from that follow but perhaps if we could get that on the record it would be prudent. I ask for just a brief moment, Mr. President, to address Your Honours and I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you. I think it's still that we're in the earlier phase, early phase of the Defence cases, I think it's worth bearing in mind some of the remarks that I hope to present to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. Judge Trechsel draws my attention to the following. Do the Defence counsel agree for the proceedings to continue without their clients? So far we haven't had any problems under such circumstances because when an accused is represented by counsel, counsel is there to represent his client and there's no absolute need for the accused to be present. Furthermore, there are instances in this Tribunal where the accused have not attended a hearing because they didn't want to, for example, and in those cases, the Trial Chamber told the counsel, well, we'll proceed anyway. What I mean to say is that the accused does not have a right per se to ask for the hearing to stop. If he wants the hearing to stop, he first has to ask the Chamber and the Chamber can agree with that or deny the application. But you've raised the issue, Mr. Stringer, so we're going to turn to the Defence counsel to ask them what they think about this. First of all, Ms. Tomic. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We are not opposed to the proceedings going ahead in the absence of Mr. Coric.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have any reasons to opposed continuation of the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you don't have to worry, Mr. Stringer. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. On Tuesday, after Mr. Karnavas completed his direct examination of the witness, there were 140 minutes available to the Prosecution is what I'm told for cross-examination. Of that 140 minutes on Tuesday that remained in the day, the Prosecution actually was able to use just 46 in cross-examination. The other time, the other 100 minutes or so being used by either the Trial Chamber or the parties. Yesterday, during the first session, the Prosecution was able to use less than half of the time that was available in the first session and I'm told that the Prosecution used about an hour of the 90 minutes in the second session, that is about two-thirds. We were able to use more time during the final session. I wanted to raise this, Mr. President, because I think at this early stage of the Defence case, it's worth reminding, respectfully, everyone that the Trial Chamber's views as expressed in the past have been to obviously it will ask questions and intervene when it deems it appropriate but the preference is that the Trial Chamber waits until all the parties have completed their examinations. I recognise that the Judges are professionals. So are the attorneys. The attorneys spend a lot of time preparing their examinations. And when lengthy and frequent interventions take substantial amounts of time away from any party and certainly I can speak on behalf of the Prosecution, it does affect the quality of the examination that occurs and I feel that my effectiveness was diminished over the course of this cross-examination because of the frequent and lengthy interventions that took place during what was supposed to be cross-examination. I recognise that the Judges will ask questions, and I can inform you that I appreciate it. I have been involved in other cases where the Judges were not nearly so active, and I can say on the behalf of the Prosecution we welcome the active involvement of the Judges in this case. I would suggest, however, that in the course of this examination, my cross-examination, the balance, that we seek and strive for has been lost or was lost, and it did have an impact; and I only make these comments now to see if we can all go back to the point we reached during an earlier phase in the Prosecution case in which everyone, I think, was going to try to exercise some restraint in respecting the other parties' abilities to lead their own examinations and those are the comments I wish to make, Mr. President. I'm not trying to be critical of anyone, but I just thought it was worth raising this issue now since we're at this early part of the Defence cases. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think a principal position must be to support generally the comments of my learned friend with one caveat, he does say at page 4, line 14, that the frequent interventions take substantial amounts of time away from a party. Of course any questions asked by the Bench are not counted as part of that time, but the point is a good one. Sometimes it is difficult to continue a flow of cross-examination or examination in chief if there are frequent interventions. Sometimes we are to blame by necessity we have to stand up and make some objections or seek some clarification. Unless there is a compelling reason or in the Trial Chamber's words, some exceptional reason, I think my learned friends points are good and I would for a principal point of view support them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, good morning. The Petkovic Defence position is no different, and we certainly would respectfully remind Your Honour that we really did have precisely the same discussion during the course of the Prosecution case and in fact it gave rise to some fairly detailed discussion and we -- Your Honours may recall we actually submitted jointly in the end Defence and Prosecution, we had agreed between ourselves what we felt were suitable guidelines for Your Honours to issue -- you, Your Honours, issue the guidelines not us and although they weren't formally issued, Your Honours did indicate that very broadly, that approach which was jointly submitted by the Prosecution and the Defence would be followed and that is all consistent with what Mr. Stringer has said this morning supported by Mr. Khan and certainly no difference from the Petkovic Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber will deliberate on this. We have taken note of your comments, and we'll let you know how we shall proceed in the future that's all I can say at the moment. However, on my personal behalf, I could respond, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would like to make a short remark. I fully understand the point raised by Mr. Stringer, and I do not wish to wash my hands in full innocence. I would like to ask back whether you would accept that we go on asking interrupting questions when they are related to a document which is actually displayed and which may then disappear and later it may be difficult to bring it back.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It's a difficult question, Mr. President or Your Honour. I used the word "balance" in my comments and I think that that's the key here. Certainly there is some advantage to taking the witness to a document when it's in front of him because it does take time to move around among the many documents. But when the practice continues extensively or repeatedly, then I think that's when the balance begins to tilt in the wrong direction and it may be that there are situations which the Trial Chamber, it is better to come back to a document if it looks as though the Trial Chamber or if an individual judge thinks that there will be perhaps a series of questions about the document. The presidential transcripts, perhaps, are a good example because when you talk about policy and conversations and some of the more complex issues, those are issues that really don't lend themselves to a yes or no question and it may be that in that situation, it's just best to come back to it later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's really just saying what Mr. Stringer said but we would say the distinction is where a fairly quick and easy resolution of some doubt or some explanation of the document can be got out of the way and that document can be done and dusted for that immediate purpose, then by all means it makes sense to go ahead; but if it's going to give rise to a line of questioning, then in exactly the same way that a cross-examiner will come back to the document that the examiner in chief has put before the Court, it should be left and exactly as Mr. Stringer says, it's not the end of the world if we come back to an important document from time to time, that's simply a necessary and essential part of the process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not going to follow-up on my fellow Judges comments because we'll consider the matter together. Let me just give you a brief word of technical explanation. At some point yesterday, I asked a question to the witness. First of all, let me say that I asked no questions of the witness during the examination in chief, I'm sure you have taken note of this. And you yourself addressed the Medjurgorje meeting and you addressed the contents of that particular document. And then I noticed that the witness had not attended the meeting but you, yourself, had not put any questions to him about it, asking: How come the ambassador who is supposed to represent his government was not even there? When I noticed that, I asked him the question. Of course I could have waited for you to complete your cross-examination before dealing with that, but let me remind you, Mr. Stringer, that we have five binders, three red binders, two of your binders. Five binders in total. Sometimes you refer to documents that are to be found in the blue binders without telling us whether they are found in binder 1, 2 or 3. So whilst you are still talking we have to turn around, find the proper binder, find the document then we have to manage to follow your questions. So does it mean that we would have to put the binders back again and retrieve them afterwards? When we have a document in front of us, I don't see why we could not ask the question immediately, whilst the document is being displayed. As for the rest, I do not agree with you but that's another matter. In any case, the Trial Chamber will consider your submissions and will tell you what our position is, but we've taken due note of your comments. We are now going to have the witness brought in. We have 1 hour and 4 minutes left, and I will try not to ask any questions during this hour and four minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: While the witness is being brought in, I wanted to ask, I had heard a rumour that the President -- there's another hearing in a different case in which the President needs to attend at 11.00 this morning and I don't know if that's correct or not or whether it's going to affect the proceedings in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, beware of rumours. There's nothing more insidious than rumours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I heard it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's all I have to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It's a good source, anyway, if it's a rumour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we heard the same rumour and raised the same question and it just -- -- Your Honour, may we know whether this rumour has any foundation at all or is simply an absurd, malicious, completely unfounded mischievous rumour because we saw an 11.00 hearing on the court schedule in a matter that seems to involve Your Honour so -- but please, is it -- can this rumour be Scotched or is there something in it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stewart, for the past two years, ever since the beginning of this trial, I have not missed a single hearing. I will be here today throughout the day. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ambassador, welcome back. I assure you we will be finished asking questions of you today. In beginning, I want to take you to a document that I referred to yesterday but I wasn't able to put my hands on at the time and with the usher's assistance, it's on the ELMO next to you right here, Mr. Ambassador. This is from the book that you wrote and this related to some remarks he made about certain segments, if you will, of the international community and I wanted to ask you a little bit about your views on that. For the record, this is from Defence Exhibit 1D02339. Perhaps if we could put it on the ELMO, at least the English version. Dr. Sancevic, underneath the English translation there, you'll find the actual excerpt from your book so why don't you just take that part and the highlighting is from someone else, it's not from me or the Prosecution so it doesn't mean anything in particular to us. But I just want to read one part of this, and then we'll go from there. You wrote in your book: "Although political squabbles contributed to the beginning of the armed conflict between the HVO and the Muslim BiH army in Central Bosnia, Rama and Mostar in the spring of 1993, I still think that the main causes were the overcrowding of Central Bosnia and the dark deeds of foreign intelligence services with the British in the lead, to whom, we have already said, it was in their interest that the Muslims and Croats would come into conflict to the benefit of the Greater Serbs. It was not a coincidence that it was the British, members of UNPROFOR who were deployed in an area where the Croats and the Muslims were the most mixed and it was precisely there that the mutual destruction was the worst, despite the fact that the mutual coexistence of the Croats and Muslims had up to that point been virtually ideal." Then you continue on with a reference to your father and some of his involvement in that area of Central Bosnia. You make a reference to the British forces of UNPROFOR that were in Central Bosnia and I wanted to ask you: Are you suggesting that it was the British forces there in Central Bosnia that are responsible for the conflicts between Croats and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not like to engage in generalisations but I must say that some of the British commanders of UNPROFOR brought along some advisors to Bosnia-Herzegovina who were Greater Serbs. For instance, the first general, General Rose, I had contacts with him in Sarajevo. General Rose was surrounded by Greater Serbs. It went so far that when a shell was fired killing great numbers of Muslims, Croats, and Serbs in Sarajevo, out of the Main Staff of General Rose, it was announced that the Muslims had been firing upon themselves. I was there. I was present. This was a horrible absurdity. I used to come to General Rose's office and talk to him there. I was aware of the people around him. It is not my intention to level accusations at General Rose. I was rather inclined toward the British individuals that I used to work with at this point and that, but I did notice that there was a large presence of Greater Serbs in the office of General Rose. My observations led me to believe that they made a significant contribution to the breaking out of the conflict between the Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And you say that they made that contribution in order to assist or to help the -- those who wanted to establish a Greater Serbia, that was your view that that was their objective?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mind you, one has to be very careful of engaging in generalizations. When we refer to the British, we need to know who precisely we are referring to. If we are referring to the conservative party of Great Britain, we will find that in that Tory party, there were those who had a full grasp of the whole issue such as Madam Margaret Thatcher who had full understanding for the problems, experienced by Bosnia-Herzegovina. I don't know where her interest stemmed from and there were those who were completely ignorant of these issues. Of course one cannot accuse them of being ignorant and of making mistakes in their full ignorance and perhaps this was the case of General Rose.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You make a reference here more specifically to the British forces that were deployed in the area of Central Bosnia British units, the members of the UNPROFOR. I wanted to ask you about that because we've had a lot of cases here in the Tribunal about the cases that happened in Central Bosnia and one of the most notorious events was the massacre that occurred in Ahmici on the 16th of April, 1993. Do you know about Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, heard about it a great deal.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that it was the British battalion, the UNPROFOR forces that were in Central Bosnia that bear some responsibility for the events, for example, in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, in my book, I'm indicating the reasons or issues that led to the conflict between the Croats and Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina. This isn't the only reason I'm mentioning, I mentioned other reasons as well, such as overcrowding. All the way until 1975, 70 per cent of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina was ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and I apologise for cutting you off but we're going to have to move a little more quickly today. My question I think is quite specific. You seem to be making an allegation here and I want to make sure that we understand correctly what it is you are alleging. Are you blaming the British battalion for the events that took place in Central Bosnia such as those in Ahmici? I think it's a yes or no question. Do they bear responsibility, in your view, or not?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not want to give you a yes or no answer because there are other reasons related to that which I mention in my book, the overcrowding, the large presence of refugees from Sandzak and so on and so forth. This is something that we established as a result of the second good will mission. We referred to the first good will mission, Turkish-Croat mission, and it was the second such mission that led us to establish the reasons that led to these conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, you're aware that it was units of the HVO that committed the acts, the crimes that were occurred in Ahmici, for example, you do know that?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, yes. There were such HVO units as committed these -- perhaps I should better not go into that, you told me not to go into too many details.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's fine. Let's just move then to the next topic. You testified about your personal involvement in the good will mission that went into Mostar, and I believe the process began in May and actually ultimately resulted in the Muslim soldiers being evacuated at some point in June of 1993. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Because I was the main player there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If I could direct you to Exhibit P2446 which is in the Prosecution binder. And while that's being found, Mr. Ambassador, this is a report of the Spanish UNPROFOR forces. You're I'm sure familiar with them because like you, they were also based in Medjurgorje. Do you recall the Spanish Battalion?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I remember the Spanish Battalion. The Spanish Battalion assisted with the evacuation of the heavily wounded Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And on page 5 of that document, of the English version, there's a reference here to the Medjurgorje delegations actually having gone to the Heliodrom facility where -- to see the Muslim prisoners. And I'm looking at the top of page 5, it says that, "After the meeting, the Croatian and Muslim representatives, a personal envoy of Lord Owen and other international organisations: ECMM, et cetera, visited the HVO detention camp situated at the heliport south-west of Mostar." My first question, Mr. Ambassador, is whether you're aware during the events of 9-10 May and beyond, hundreds of Muslim civilians were arrested throughout the Mostar area and were taken out and put into detention at the Heliodrom facility. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not at Heliodrom, I was in Dretelj, but I believe that you're referring to the same problem in both cases. What would you like me to tell but all that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Just simply my question was whether, during this time of the Medjurgorje process, were you aware that hundreds of Muslims had been arrested and placed in detention south of Mostar? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned about that through New York Times.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I immediately informed Zagreb about that. I informed my superior, Dr. Mate Granic about that, who immediately transmitted the problem to Dr. Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You're talking about the prison camp at Dretelj?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Were you aware that there was a different prison camp where Muslims were held at a place called the Heliodrom that was outside of Mostar, close to Mostar? Were you aware of that place?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of a number of different prisons where Muslims were kept, where Croats were kept and - how should I put it - the -- I was aware of the HVO prisons where Muslims were kept. All of that was a result of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, if Muslim civilians had been arrested and rounded up and placed in detention, I take it that you would not support such a process -- or any civilians for that matter.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, there must have been different situations and cases involved. I'm not talking only about civilians because when I visited Dretelj, I spoke to everybody who wanted to have a word. I was together with Dr. Mato Granic, we visited Dretelj and --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm asking in general terms, and I am asking about civilians.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not tell the difference between the two because there are a lot of Muslims who were members of the HVO as well and I believe, this is just my opinion, I cannot claim this for a fact and say that this was an absolute truth. I believe that with regard to the attempt by General Arif Pasalic to break through to the sea brought about lots of mistrust towards the Muslims who were members of the HVO. All I'm saying that as a result of that, the situation for them was not very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me just take a question. First I want to go back to my last question. I was asking about Muslim civilians arrested and placed in detention, civilians, people who were not a member of the HVO or the Armija. Would you agree with me that it was improper and that you would not support detaining civilians --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. Witness, please, do not answer because I see that Ms. Tomic is on her feet. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you for giving me this opportunity to intervene. I have refrained from intervening but I have to do it at this time. Yesterday and today, on several occasions, the witness has repeated that his knowledge refers only to some general and wildly inane facts. This is a topic that goes beyond the scope of direct examination, beyond the briefing notes, this is now a new issue being opened, no single Defence has cross-examined on this, they could not have because otherwise this would have been direct examination. On several occasions, the witness has repeated that whatever he knows about Heliodrom he learned from the New York Times. Now he's being asked to provide his valued judgement which is not up to this witness to do. I believe that the appropriate question would be to ask the witness what he read in the New York Times, although I don't know how this may be relevant. He has repeated on several occasions that whatever he learns about Heliodrom comes from the New York Times. We don't even know when he read it because the Prosecutor never asked him that. I believe that this is nothing but a torture of this witness. This may be a too strong word but it all boils down to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We're going to talk about Dretelj and the New York Times article later that happens in September of 1993, and I'm still in May of 1993 and I'm still in Mostar and that's what I'm wanting to talk about. In general, I think these issues relate to the witness' credibility. If he's part of this Medjurgorje process and he doesn't know anything about the Heliodrom, I think that bears somewhat on his credibility, and I'm trying to test him in terms of what he knows about the situation that was unfolding in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you will allow me. Since we have already interrupted my learned friend's examination, all this time, he has been comparing i.e., drawing a parallel between the Medjurgorje process and the situation at the Heliodrom. For that reason, I would like to draw your attention to the evidence that was presented before the -- this Trial Chamber saying that the meeting in Medjurgorje was on the 18th of May, 1993, and that we have documents both from the BiH army and the UNPROFOR showing that on that day, all civilians who had been kept at the Heliodrom were released, so I believe it is not founded to compare the two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Stringer, you told us that in fact you're putting all these questions to the witness because of his credibility and this is why you are asking questions with regards to the people who were in the -- or at the Heliodrom is to test his credibility. Is this what we should understand?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's correct. I think if things are happening that he doesn't know about, it impacts the witness 'credibility in the terms of the opinions he's expressed. I don't intend to spend a great deal of time, I don't have a lot of time but I think a few questions on this are appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please go ahead. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So Mr. Ambassador, you've indicated you didn't go to the Heliodrom, and I think it's fair to say you're not very familiar with it so we'll just leave it at that. One other question, a couple more questions, I should say about the events that were happening in Mostar before we move on to Dretelj. Were you aware throughout the summer of 1993 that there was a very large-scale campaign by which the Muslims of west Mostar were forced out of their apartments and their flats and they were made either to leave Mostar or to move across the river into east Mostar? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my conversation with people in Dretelj, when people saw that their ambassador of the Republic of Croatia had come, they rallied around me and asked me different questions. I just wanted to put the whole situation in context. I was accompanying Dr. Mate Granic, the Minister of Foreign Affairs and I was accompanying the International Red Cross that was involved in the whole situation. In those conversations, some of those people in Dretelj told me that they had been members of the HVO, they were Muslims, and they asked not to be transferred to the other side, to the BiH army side because they feared a retaliation by the other Muslims against those Muslims who had fought among the ranks of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So apart from the people that you spoke to at Dretelj, you don't know anything about whether large numbers of Muslims families were being evicted from their apartments in west Mostar and forced across the river into east Mostar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not in a position to quantify anything, but I was in contact with the Muslims who had spent the entire war in Mostar. I'm sure that you have documents about Mr. Hadziosmanovic and so on and so forth who was in Mostar, so you cannot say in general terms that all the Muslims were chased away. There must have been those who wanted to leave, there must have been those who came into conflict with the HVO and there was also a fraction of Muslims who remained in Mostar all that time just like the gentleman whom I've just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So if there was wide scale ethnic cleansing of Muslims from west Mostar, you don't know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I object to the term "widespread ethnic cleansing." Now if he could lay down the facts as to who said what to establish these facts, I haven't objected because I don't want to interrupt the gentleman, but I don't support the facts that he's using to base his questions on. So obviously there were some evictions, but now he's talking about widespread, he's talking about policies. If he could quote who said what so we could have exactly in the evidence where does he get these -- this final argument that he's putting into this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's fine. Mr. President, I can take the witness to a document but we'll need to go into closed session for just a few minutes about it because it's the a document under seal -- or private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I'm sorry, counsel, Your Honours, we are back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, the next exhibit is marked P05219, 5219 it's in the Prosecution binder --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Binder 1 or 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It's in the first binder, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, this is a document that's a report by a different international organisation that was in the region called the European Community Monitoring Mission. They had people who were down in the region making reports and this is one of their reports, and it's dated the 20th of September, 1993 and it's talking about Mr. Granic's visit down to Grude when there were discussions about closing the camps and other things and that's what I want to ask you about now. First of all, were you -- did you accompany Mr. Granic down to Grude when these discussions took place about Dretelj?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not with Dr. Granic at the time, but I was in Dretelj with Dr. Granic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, as you've indicated previously, you, I take it, became aware of the Dretelj issue because of an article that was published in the New York Times; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember a time whether the article -- whether the article mentions Dretelj, but I know that some camps were mentioned in the article. Do you have the article here to show it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I don't have the article, I just mentioned it because I thought you had mentioned the New York Times. Is it fair to say, then, that there were press reports about the issue of camps and that was what drew your attention to this issue for the first time? Is that a correct way to put it?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, because I don't have the article with me either, so as far as I can remember --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. I'm really sorry to interrupt you, Ambassador Sancevic and also Mr. Stringer but since it is a document now we are talking about and -- when should we intervene when we want to say that since Ambassador Sancevic said that that time he was not with Minister Granic there but on the other hand there in the document itself, page -- the second page actually, among the participants we do have his name, I believe, it's the last one here, Dr. Zdravko Sancevic, Croatian ambassador to the Republic of Herceg-Bosna. It is ambassador to the Republic of Herceg-Bosna so therefore, I believe, Mr. Sancevic, you had to be there because of the participants of -- to that meeting, you are also listed in. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember that I was there and what place is that? At that place when Granic and Boban met, but I remember very well that I accompanied Dr. Granic to Dretelj.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Just actually right after your name in the report, the report continues by saying that it indicates that after the meeting took place, then, "The meeting moved to Dretelj and were given a conducted tour of the camp. So that's the part that you know about for sure that you were part of the group that went to the camp itself.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, precisely as stated here. The meeting moved on to Dretelj and I was present there. Unfortunately, I don't recall being present during the meeting of the Minister of Foreign Affairs, Dr. Mate Granic and Mr. Boban.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, sir, that when Dr. Granic heard about this particular camp, he was of the view that it should be closed and that it was in the interests of Croatia itself to get this camp closed?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only that camp, all camps. Muslim camps with Croatian detainees or any other prison for that matter where Muslims may have been held on the 18th of May in the agreement, it was stated that all existing prisons should be eliminated, reciprocally.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In this report, it indicates actually that Mr. Granic went as far to say that this particular camp at Dretelj would be closed unilaterally with the help of the International Committee Red Cross, do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And that's because the conditions of the Dretelj camp were seen to be as particularly bad?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to tell the truth. How can I assess whether it was particularly bad? For some of the people I talked to, the situation was bad whereas for others, it wasn't. There were some jovial people there. They knew that they were to be set free, that it was all provisional and so on and so forth. I cannot generalise, I am very much against general statements of any sort. I spoke with the people I did and that is what I can tell you as being the truth and that is something I can tell you specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Just a few questions about the camp and the people you spoke to. Do you know, in fact, that these people -- tell us if you know why were they in the camp? What had they done to be put in this camp? Do you know why they were there?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conflicts between certain Croatian and certain Muslim units resulted in the taking of prisoners. That is where the situation stemmed from. Both sides had locations, prisons for detainees. In a previous statement of mine, I said that there were no prisons in Herceg-Bosna. Once the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was formed, I was witness to the fact that all the prisons had been disbanded. Later on they were reopened because of the conflicts of certain units on both sides. There were prisons on the side of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina as well as on the side of the HVO. Now, I can't tell you how many, why, who was held there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. My question was why they were being held there, and you have just indicated that you can't tell us why.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that when there is a conflict, such things happen; however, I cannot tell you why someone was detained. There may have been reasons of all sorts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Were you aware that there was some 500 or so of these prisoners who were so malnourished that they were taken out and they were actually taken down to Croatia toward Korcula where they were placed in a refugee camp off the coast of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know that some went to Korcula; however, I'm not aware of the fact that they may have been malnourished. I don't know what their physical condition was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So you didn't see any prisoners there who appeared to be in bad shape physically?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Listen, again, a generalisation. Within a group of people, some people are in poor physical condition, some are sick, but then there are those who are perfectly fit. As far as I could see, I saw that most of them were normal people; however, that some of them were sick.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You indicated that Dr. Granic's view was that the camp was to be closed unilaterally. Does that mean that all the prisoners were going to be released then or transferred down towards Korcula?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was definitely not so. Please let me explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I was just -- if the prisoners were not being released then where were they going to go from Dretelj, if you know? If you don't know, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, do give me a context. I cannot answer questions like these taken out of the context. Both Dr. Granic and Dr. Tudjman --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you can't demand from the Prosecutor that he ask his question in a specific context. The Prosecutor is entitled to put questions to you. When you answer, you are perfectly entitled to give the background and say: "I'm going to answer your question, but remember that the situation was as follows ..." but then you have to answer the question in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The context was that Dr. Granic had said the prison was to be closed unilaterally. I'm asking you: Do you know, then, what was to become of the prisoners there?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First and foremost, they were to be taken out of the prison. Your Honour, if I intend to tell the truth and nothing but the truth, there's something I need to add to my answer. Why did Dr. Granic go there at all? That's not what you asked me about. Why was it that it was decided unilaterally to set those people free.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's not one of my questions and I'm the one who gets to ask the questions at this point. If one of the Judges or one of the other parties wants to ask you that question, but I've sort of moved on from that and I've only got a limited amount of time left to me; so I'd like to stay with this particular question of the release or the transfer of the prisoners. Mr. Ambassador, you said that they were to be taken out of the prison. My question is: Do you know where they would go?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It was a matter for discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next exhibit is P05312, Prosecution binder which -- that's in the first Prosecution binder. I want to ask you -- MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] I apologise to my learned friend. I see that the Chamber did not see me standing up. Another objection. This document has already been exhibited. I wanted to say this: This question and those that will come, and I know more or less in what direction the Prosecutor is moving, will this have to do with the credibility of the witness because I believe we are wasting time. What the witness said he knew about the prison situation is something he already gave his statement about. He testified about it the day before yesterday, yesterday, and today, he says he was not familiar with any details, he was familiar with only the general situation and that his formal knowledge pertains to one visit to one particular prison. He wasn't familiar with the structure of the HVO or of Herceg-Bosna because he dealt with issues at a higher level with the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as far as I understood. I believe he was very clear on that. I think through the issue of credibility, an issue is being brought in through the back door on which the Defence did not have any opportunity to cross-examine. Any of us could have raised that topic or any topic from the indictment, for that matter, and we could spend 10 hours or each and then it would be taken off our time and treated as direct examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, you are still testing the witness' credibility, are you? You've asked him what had become of the prisoners, he's saying that he doesn't know and you're trying to test his answer with this particular document. Is that the way you're going about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, just further in terms of what practices he was aware of and what practices he was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is well beyond the scope of direct examination. Again, I don't want to -- I do not want to interrupt but I would join with my colleague at the conclusion before I do my redirect, I would ask that the Court allow my colleagues to do their direct examination based on the cross-examination of the Prosecution because he's going into areas which we did not go in. He was an ambassador, he had nothing to do with the prisoners. Now he's being asked some questions about issues that he has no knowledge of. So it's well beyond the scope of direct examination. Actually, we're going to clear this up on redirect but it's quite obvious. It's quite obvious that he had nothing to do with where anybody was being transferred, the camps, the prisoners, or any of that sort. So why are we going into this and I would suggest that if you allow this line of questioning then it's fair to at least the Coric Defence and others, perhaps, to open up and then I get to do a redirect on the basis of what we hear from the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just with your leave, one additional observation. From my part, I'm not sure about the cogency of the submissions with respect about this going to credibility but be that as it may, under Rule 90(H) as this was not a matter that was raised in examination in chief, the only grounds in my respectful submission to allow further questioning is if Your Honours are satisfied that this witness is capable of giving relevant evidence in relation to this document and of course for that, my learned friend has to establish a foundation either that he's seen the document, it was addressed to him, the usual foundations have to be laid. I don't actually see this going to matters of credibility at all, but I do have concerns about the ability of this witness to give relevant evidence in relation to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, first of all, this document has already been admitted into evidence so nothing to do with reliability or relevance. This has already been adjudicated because the document has been admitted into evidence so this has nothing to do with the particular fact that five individuals were transferred from one prison to the next. So why are you putting this document to the witness? Is it because you want to address the issue of the prisoners and that was not raised during direct examination and it's a new area you're dealing with or are you dealing with the credibility of the witness, a witness who goes to Dretelj and who has no idea what has become of people who were released. So what -- why are you putting this document to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It's precisely the second point that Your Honour just raised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It seems to me, Mr. Stringer, that the witness has clearly said he has no idea, he does not know what happens to prisoners that were taken out of Dretelj, so I do not see how further questions relating to the same fact could bring anything, either information or anything as to credibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, I'll obviously accept whatever ruling comes from the Trial Chamber on this. I'm at the very end -- this is essentially the last of the cross-examination, and I can finish this within the next five to ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine, the objection is sustained so I'm going to ask you to move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. I'm just taking a moment to look over my notes, Mr. President. It may be that I've finished. Mr. Ambassador, thank you for your time. I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We are going to take the break, but with respect to redirect, the Trial Chamber would like to say the following to Mr. Karnavas in order to avoid any useless discussions. Today, the Trial Chamber will file its written decision for clarification of the guidelines and not to modify the guidelines, we are going to clarify the meaning of the guidelines. I would therefore like to invite you to read our decision that will probably be filed today. Under the guidelines, the time we allocated to you based on the time you requested, 4 hours for this witness, this amount of time for us includes both direct examination and re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That is the Trial Chamber's decision and again I must object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait, wait, please wait.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Because I think it's a fundamentally flawed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, you are to sit down and listen until the president has finished explaining.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But the calculating period of -- in that fashion is fundamentally flawed. Now if you're going to give me something that I'm already entitled to as some sort of a gift, I object to that. Four hours is four hours for direct. You cannot predict how much redirect and that's why I object as a matter of principle. I'm not here like some beggar. My client has rights, he has the right to redirect. Nobody during the Prosecution case applied this procedure it's being applied solely for the Prlic Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please can you check why, when I press on this button to cut off Mr. Karnavas's mike it doesn't work. I wanted to stop Mr. Karnavas because he was discourteous. He interrupted me whilst I was giving him explanation. This is something I'm going to seize the Chamber with to see if we need to take any measures, any sanctions. Let me proceed with my explanations. Let me remind you that the time allocated to you includes both direct examination and re-examination. If the Defence wants additional time for additional questions, the Trial Chamber shall automatically grant that additional time but the Trial Chamber will deduct that additional time from the overall amount of time allocated to the Defence. In other words, Mr. Prlic's Defence was given 95 hours in total. This amount of time cannot be changed. If today, as part of a redirect, Mr. Prlic's Defence uses one hour, he will have in total 95 hours minus one hour minus the time already used. If you want to spend 10 hours re-examining the witness, you are entitled to do so, if you want to spend 20 hours re-examining a witness, you are perfectly entitled to do so, but all the time thus spent will be deducted from the overall time allocated to you because time dedicated to re-examination is not going to be added to time that was allocated to you in the first place. Let me remind you and that's something I set out in my personal opinion and that's also a view shared by the Trial Chamber that we established the time allocated to each Defence team based on 65 ter lists submitted by the various Defence teams and in that list, you indicated how much time you needed for each one of your witnesses. We took all that into account when allocating you a specific amount of time. When we made that decision, it was not by pure chance, it was after countless hours of work, of review of all the elements in order to establish the guidelines. You requested clarification of these guidelines, this is going to be done in writing and the decision is going to be filed today, but since we're here in the middle of a testimony, I just wanted to confirm that to you. In other words, you are entitled, you're perfectly entitled to put additional questions to the witness, but if you spend 30 hours in re-examination, that will be deducted from your time. If you spend an hour, it will be deducted from your time as well. It's for you to decide. I already stated last week that when a witness comes here to testify, you have to anticipate how much time you will need for redirect and reserve maybe 30 minutes out of four hours for redirect. You can know in advance -- you know in advance what sort of questions you will ask. You know what sort of questions that will be put during cross-examination and on that basis, you can have an estimate of time needed for re-examination. But please, Mr. Karnavas, please, when someone is speaking, please let them finish rather than jumping on your feet and start intervening when you have no idea what they will be saying. When you are talking, I let you finish, I don't cut you off because if I did so I may not understand what you're driving at. Yes, I must admit that in the past I cut you off, but it was just because you had intervened while someone else was saying; but it's common courtesy to let people speak out. That's why the presiding judge has this button here to cut off anybody's mike here. I tried to use it but it didn't work, unfortunately. Now we're going to have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I apologise to the Court for the interruption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apologies accepted, Mr. Karnavas, gladly accepted. Rest assured that I understand the necessities you're working under, but the Judges also have to obey a number of requirements and sometimes these requirements are not exactly the same but that's not good enough cause to get all worked up and not to remain quiet. I tried to remain as calm as I can in courtroom. Sometimes it's not easy, I have to get a hold of myself. It can be very difficult at times but I try to do so as everybody else in this courtroom. Let's have a 20-minute break and then we'll resume the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It is almost 11.00. I am here, as you can see. This will allow me to read a short oral decision on a request presented by Mr. Kovacic. Oral decision on the nature of the cross-examination of Adalbert Rebic by the private Defence. During the cross examination of the Witness Rebic on the 21st of May, 2008, Mr. Kovacic raised a topic that was raised during the direct examination regarding the work made by the VAP agency for the ODPR of the Republic of Croatia. Mr. Kovacic then expanded this topic and talked about humanitarian convoys organized by Mr. Binenfeld, director of the VAP agency going towards Sarajevo. During the hearing of the 21st of May 2008, the Chamber ruled that humanitarian convoys going towards Sarajevo, that this topic was a new topic as you say in your own language, novatema [phoen] and that under guideline number 6, paragraph 20, this time should have been deducted from the total time allocated to the Defence of Mr. Praljak to present its case. The Chamber maintains this decision and confirms that the portion of the cross-examination led by Mr. Kovacic that can be found on the French transcript starting on page 28326, line 21 to page 28327, line 15 which deals with the topic of humanitarian convoys going to Sarajevo is a matter that had not been raised during the direct examination. The time used for that question, one minute or 60 seconds is therefore deducted from the allocated time given to the Praljak Defence to present its case. Very well. I certainly hope that this will not severely violate the rights of Mr. Praljak's Defence. For these reasons, we are now going or rather we are going to put some questions -- yes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Karnavas during the break, I had one clarification to make for the record. I erroneously said that I was directing the witness to a part of his book that was marked as Exhibit 1D02339. I was wrong. The correct exhibit number I should have said is 1D02808 so just so that that's in the record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Mr. Karnavas, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I have a few questions, not many. And presumably if you answer them rather directly and shortly, we'll be able to get out of here within the next 15 or 20 minutes. My first topic is to go back to the 18 May 1993 meeting in Medjurgorje because there seems to be some contradiction in the transcript. On the first day, on Monday, the 26th, you indicated and this is on transcript page -- it would be 39 of Monday's transcript. I asked you concretely whether you had been there and you said yes. Then again, a reference was made to it on page 44 of Monday's transcript. Then, I believe you were asked by the Prosecutor, and I believe that was on page -- and this would be 28.775 line 18, and again, on 28.776, line 22, you again indicated that you had indeed been present during the Medjurgorje meeting on 18 May 1993. You were then questioned by President Antonetti, and I believe this is on page 28.782 lines 1 to 14 and whether you had been at the meeting and this came up when it was shown -- when document P02441, P02441 was shown to you where your name is not listed as one of the participants. So just concretely and can we -- I just want to clarify this matter: Were you or were you not present during that meeting? And it's a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, and of course you indicated that there had been a meeting prior to that in Split and were you present during that meeting at the Split meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, let me touch upon one area that was brought up today and that had to do with the camps. We know that you were an ambassador. You've told us, so I'm not leading you, this is part of your testimony, that from the time you presented your credentials up until approximately August 1993, you were more or less in a roving capacity headquartered more or less out of Neum while at the same time spending sometime in Croatia when not travelling around; is that correct? Did I get it right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, was your remit at that point in time to deal with anything that had to deal with prisoners --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please, Mr. Karnavas. A small language precision. You see -- I see that in English, you say "camp" and in French, the translation that I get is "camp," so what does "camp" mean in English, really?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I can turn it into a detention centre, prison, I'm using that interchangeably. I mean, but we'll talk about detention centres. How is that it's a more neutral --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... to deal with any of the detention centres while you were ambassador during that period up until the time that you set up your Medjurgorje embassy?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, after visiting Dretelj with Dr. Granic who was your superior, after all, he was the Minister of Foreign Affairs, did Dr. Granic in any way instruct you personally, that is, as the ambassador of Croatia to Bosnia-Herzegovina to get involved with any issues dealing with detention centres, prisoners, or what have you?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's move on to the next topic. Yesterday, you were asked a series of questions by the Prosecutor concerning your contact with Dr. Jadranko Prlic and at one point, the question was, I believe something to the effect that aside from speaking to him about matters of economics, whether you had any discussions on substantive issues and you did speak about -- you went back and you clarified that there were conversations that you had that dealt with matters of economics. First of all, I want to touch on that. Did -- perhaps we can look at, for instance, 1D02186. 1D02186. It's in the Defence binder. It's in the Defence binder. Which one, I can't tell you. One. If we can give him the hard copies, Mr. Usher, if we can provide hard copies, it might be easier this way. Now, before I -- we go into this document, as I understand it, when we talked about your qualifications, I indicated that you had worked for Shell and as I understand, you also worked for Atlantic Richfield, the oil company as well?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In your capacity, I know you were a petroleum engineer holding a Ph.D in that field, did you hold any management positions so you would be acquainted with matters dealing with business, economics, that sort of stuff?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I dealt with these matters and occupied high positions. I was vice-president and president of, for instance --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the name of the company.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You were vice-president and president of what company? Could you repeat it, please?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And what kind of company is that?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] that's a national [Interpretation] Bariven is the nationalised Atlantic Richfield and Sinclair. Once they were nationalised, I became first vice-president and then for a short while, I was president, CEO of that company as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's in Venezuela?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in Venezuela.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if you look at this document, 1D02186, it's dated April 15th, 1993 and of course this is addressed to Jadranko Prlic, and it's in regards to the matter of establishing a banking system which will be part of the banking system of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in keeping with the solutions provided by the Vance-Owen agreement and we can see further down it talks about central bank, regional banks, bank investment funds and this of course comes from the chief of the finance department. My first question -- well my only question regarding this document is, sir, were these the sort of -- was this the sort of topic that you had with Dr. Jadranko Prlic concerning the banking system discussions related to those issues, finance, banking? Is that one of topics?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. The next document is 1D02231. This is dated 22 April 1993, and we can see from the topics this is in relation to a conference that is being held, it's an academic conference at the Hotel Sunce in Neum and it deals with matters of economics. Were you present at this particular conference or were you aware of Dr. Prlic's involvement in this conference?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a clear idea of what was happening at the time because I stayed in the building which belonged to the Mostar University. I knew Dr. Zdenko Kordic, the director of the university, and I was interested in seeing the upshot of that although I did not take part in that conference throughout its duration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Just to make sure that we're clear, the Mostar University was actually physically located in the Sunce Hotel; is that correct? This is where also you were also residing. That's where you were operating out of?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not the Sunce Hotel, I think the name of the hotel was Neum. I lived in Neum, and this event took place in the Sunce Hotel, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You were physically located where the Mostar University was located; is that correct? That's where you were staying?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, let's go to the next document, 1D02221 because I believe you've --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, while the document's being found, Mr. President, I'd just like to make an objection for the record. Counsel's referring to documents here that were always in his binder that were not gone into on the direct examination, and I think that, yes, I followed up on something from direct related to his discussions with Mr. Prlic about economics; but I think that what's happening now is that we're just doing additional direct examination rather than remaining within the scope of something that was pretty limited on cross-examination. We're just using the witness now to tender additional documents that could have been tendered in the direct. So my objection is this: If counsel intends to tender these exhibits, the Prosecution will be objecting on the basis that this as well as the testimony is beyond the scope of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In my response, the Prosecutor is correct they were in the binder, and we didn't tender them at the time; however, when the Prosecutor stood up and said you talked to him about economics but did you speak to him about anything of substance and you may recall my objection was that what Dr. Prlic was involved with was matter of economics which are substantive matters and now we're having -- I'm following up on my objection to the Prosecution's question. I'll leave it up to the Trial Chamber to decide whether I'm going beyond the scope of direct, and if I am, I'll move on to the next subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber deliberated on this matter and believes that while putting questions in redirect, Mr. Karnavas can put questions since, during the cross-examination, a question relating on economy topics was put so this subject can be raised in redirect but the Trial Chamber has a small reserve regarding the previous document, not the one that we are seeing now on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And if I may clarify, we don't see what the link is between the previous document and Mr. Prlic. What is the connection? This is why we think it goes beyond the scope whereas here you are in fact talking about contacts that existed between the accused and the witness on substantial matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, it's sort of a -- to borrow a term in the documents, it sorts of a global nature of the issues of economics that if the Trial Chamber, however, wishes for me to move on, I'll move on. There certainly will be other witnesses discussing these issues, but I wanted to drive the point home that these are issues of substance and because the gentleman has -- I mean keeping in mind that his background, western educated as well during that period, one would understand why Dr. Prlic would want to be discussing these sorts of issues with the ambassador at the time, but I can move on. I leave it up to the Court's -- because the other two documents relate to published articles by Mr. Prlic, one dated 13 June 1993, that's 1D02221, and 1D02220 dated 2 July 1993. I leave it up to you. My question would be basically was the gentleman aware of these articles at the time that they were written given that he was having contacts with Mr. Prlic in relation to his discussions on the economic activities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, sir. I'm waiting for the translation for you. Okay. If you could just look at the next two documents, 1D02221 and 1D02220. If we could have the assistance of the usher. Just briefly, if you could just glance at them and tell us whether you had an opportunity back then to read what Dr. Prlic was publishing at the time concerning his ideas in relation to how to get the economy going during and after the war.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout that time, that's what I was doing because I thought that Mr. Prlic was very knowledgeable about these matters, and I closely followed whatever he had to say on these matters, I read the articles he wrote, and the books he authored and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we're going to switch to another topic and this relates to the law on citizenship. I just have a couple of questions because it did come up on cross-examination and this is -- I'm going to refer to the document 1D02918, 2918, realising that there are two other documents that 2919 and 2920, which are amendments but by and large the discussion will focus on the law on Croatian citizenship. Now, my first question, sir, is we saw that as of 1999 up until today, you hold a particular position in Venezuela and that is the consulate, the General Consul for the Republic of Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, in that capacity, may I ask, do you issue passports or are you involved, is your consulate involved there in any way with issuing passports or in processing documents concerning citizenship?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, as far as I understand, but correct me if I am wrong, the law that is -- that you apply today would have been the same law that we discussed earlier on direct examination and cross-examination; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was this one law in force throughout that time and then there were two amendments and now I believe that there's a third one but all of them are in accordance with the basic legislation. What I'm saying is that this law was in force throughout the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And my question is: In your capacity as General Consul in Venezuela, are you applying the law any differently now, you know, throughout this period, 1999 to present, than you were -- you had set up the embassy for the Republic of Croatia in Medjurgorje, I believe, as of August 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The law was the same one as today and I adhered to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But -- all right. Now, back then, when you were applying it, and we're talking August 1993 and thereafter, were you ever given any specific instructions either by the Minister of Foreign Affairs, and I know that you had two ministers during your tenure, as to how to apply this? In other words, was there a policy?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, what was the policy? And I'm saying was there a policy that you were instructed by the ministers: This is how you have to apply this particular law? Or were you just applying it the way you interpreted it?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I applied it the way I interpreted it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Were you ever instructed to use discriminatory methods in the application of the law, that is, in determining who should or should not become a Croatian citizen?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I believe the witness' testimony was that the citizenship applications were sent to Zagreb where they were then processed, so I didn't have the impression that the witness himself was making the ultimate decisions on granting of citizenship.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If there is a concession on the part of the Prosecution that the gentleman at least in his application of the -- for Croatian citizenships and for passports was absolutely correct and consistent with the law, then I will move on. So do I have a concession on the record?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: No, I'm just --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Hence why I'm doing my redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. I will intervene following this objection. Mr. Karnavas is asking the following question to the witness as a consul in Caracas, did he receive any particular instructions on the way to apply the law on Croatian citizenship? Then he is asking the witness that when applying the law, and particularly with regard to the issuing of passports, should something be done in particular when a passport is issued? And then the Prosecutor objects by saying, yes, but the witness stated that he would send the applications to Zagreb. The Prosecutor forgot that the issuing of passports can take place in a consulate and that for that reason, to deliver a passport, you don't have to send the application to Zagreb and the consul can tell us if, yes or no and whether he delivers or issues a passport he can verify if a person is a Croatian citizen or not, so that's basically if I thought I understood Mr. Karnavas's questions, that's the case, Mr. Karnavas please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I will try -- and also I will keep in mind the Prosecution's concerns.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Focussing now on August 1993, in processing the applications for citizenship, were you ever instructed to use discriminatory methods in order to exclude some individuals or to include others?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never received such instruction. I abided by the law. There were no particular instructions, discriminatory or otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And can I accept from that answer that President Tudjman did not instruct you, Gojko Susak did not instruct you, Granic didn't instruct you, Skrabalo didn't instruct you, none of these individuals ever instructed you. You were just doing your job based on your understanding of the application of the law; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, in keeping a little bit with this issue because the issue of transit visas and passports and documentation, I want to take you back to when you left Croatia, I believe, and then you went to Italy with your family, and then you eventually went to Venezuela. Did you, at the time, have a Croatian passport, you and your father and your mother, siblings. Did you hold a Croatian passport at the time, we were's talking about 1947 now, and I think it was 1949 when you left for Venezuela?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And what kind of document, did you have a Yugoslav passport?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, how did you get into Venezuela if you didn't have a passport from Croatia or from Yugoslavia? And I should have asked you, did you have one from Bosnia-Herzegovina? How did you get into Venezuela?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I entered Venezuela with my passport -- with just one document, travel document. The whole family used just one document that had been issued by the International Red Cross and IRO, the International Refugee Organisation which later became UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to make sure because it says here on line 5 that you "... entered Venezuela with my passport," you did not have a passport at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not have one at the time. I arrived with my parents and we all shared one piece of paper, one document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And when was the first time that you were eligible to actually obtain a Croatian passport?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in a position to obtain a Croatian passport from the moment I arrived in Croatia, but I was a Venezuelan citizen. I had a Venezuelan passport until the moment I obtained a Croatian passport.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Can you be more precise? The folks living in the diaspora, the Croats, when was it -- when was the first time that they could actually obtain a Croatian -- a passport, in the history of Croatia, the modern history of it?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC [Resumed]
